questions.q: A primary source is
o: information you collect first-hand, e.g. a survey you run
questions.why: Secondary sources are others' work.

questions.q: The most reliable source on a medical claim is usually
questions.why: Peer review checks methods and evidence.

questions.q: Which is the best first step in research?
o: Write a clear question to investigate
questions.why: A focused question guides your sources.

questions.q: A student wants to find out how far students at their school travel each day. Which method would give the most useful data?
o: Reading a national newspaper article on transport
A short questionnaire given to a sample of students from every year group
Searching social media for posts about travel
questions.why: A questionnaire to a sample across all year groups gives first-hand data that represents the whole school.

questions.q: A student is researching plastic pollution in a local river. Which of these is a secondary source?
o: Their own count of plastic items on the riverbank
A government report on the river's water quality
An interview they carried out with a local fisherman
Photographs they took along the river
questions.why: A secondary source was produced by someone else; the other three are data the student collected first-hand.

long.q: A student wants to find out how much food is wasted at their school. Suggest a suitable method for gathering this information, and explain one strength and one weakness of your method. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a suitable, specific method (e.g. weighing food left on plates in the canteen each day; a survey of students)
B1: method detailed enough to carry out (who, when, for how long, how it is recorded)
B1: a strength explained (e.g. weighing gives accurate first-hand data, not opinion)
B1: a weakness explained (e.g. one week may not be typical; students may not answer a survey honestly)

long.q: A student is investigating air quality near their school. Explain the difference between primary and secondary research, giving one example of each that the student could use. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: primary research is information the student collects first-hand for this investigation
B1: a suitable primary example, e.g. counting vehicles passing the gate at set times; a questionnaire about asthma or breathing problems
B1: secondary research is information already collected and published by someone else
B1: a suitable secondary example, e.g. the local council's air-quality readings; a government or NGO report on pollution

long.q: In a survey of 200 students at one school, 120 said they walk or cycle to school, 50 come by car and 30 come by bus. (a) Calculate the percentage of these students who come by car. (b) State one conclusion the student could draw from the data. (c) Explain one reason why the results might not represent all students in the town. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (b) a valid conclusion, e.g. most of these students (60%) walk or cycle; car is the second most common way of travelling
B1: (c) a reason explained, e.g. only one school was surveyed, and its catchment may be smaller or closer to the centre than other schools'

long.q: Read these three statements. (i) 'In 2023 the town recycled 38% of its household waste.' (ii) 'Recycling is the most important thing a family can do for the planet.' (iii) 'The council should double the number of recycling bins.' (a) For each statement, say whether it is a fact or an opinion. (b) Explain how a researcher could check the statement that is a fact. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (i) fact (it can be measured and checked)
B1: (ii) opinion and (iii) opinion: both are judgements, not checkable claims
B1: (b) look for the figure in an official source, e.g. the council's published waste statistics
B1: (b) compare it with a second, independent source, or check how the 38% was measured

long.q: A student includes this question in a survey about diet: 'Don't you agree that fast food is unhealthy?' Explain two problems with this question and rewrite it so it would give more useful results. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: it is a leading question: the wording pushes people towards agreeing, so answers are biased
B1: a second problem, e.g. it only allows yes/no, so it says nothing about how often people eat fast food; 'unhealthy' is vague
B1: a neutral, specific rewrite, e.g. 'How many times a week do you eat fast food? 0 / 1–2 / 3–4 / 5 or more'

questions.q: A 'perspective' is
o: a point of view shaped by experience and values
questions.why: GP asks you to compare personal, local, national and global perspectives.

questions.q: What is a consequence?
o: A result or effect of an issue
questions.why: Explain links between causes, consequences and possible courses of action.

questions.q: Why consider different perspectives (personal, local/national, global)?
o: Issues affect people at different scales in different ways
questions.why: Compare them to reach a judgement.

questions.q: Many young people move from rural areas to cities to find work. Which of these is a consequence of this migration rather than a cause?
o: There are few jobs in rural areas
Rural villages are left with an ageing population
Rural schools offer a limited range of courses
questions.why: An ageing village population results from young people leaving; the other options are reasons why they leave.

questions.q: Which statement is written from a national perspective?
o: I am worried I will not find a job when I leave school.
Our country's youth unemployment rate has risen to 15% this year.
The factory in our town closed last month.
Youth unemployment is rising in many countries around the world.
questions.why: It describes the issue at the level of one country; the others are personal, local and global perspectives.

long.q: Explain two causes of increasing traffic congestion in many cities and one consequence of it, from either a local or a global perspective. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: first cause explained (e.g. rising car ownership as incomes grow, so more vehicles share the same roads)
B1: a second, different cause explained (e.g. poor or expensive public transport, so people choose to drive)
B1: a consequence identified (e.g. air pollution, longer journeys, lost working time)
B1: the consequence explained from the stated perspective (local: residents' health; global: emissions adding to climate change)

long.q: Many young people are moving from rural areas to cities. Explain one consequence of this for the rural areas they leave and one consequence for the cities they move to. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a rural consequence identified, e.g. fewer workers for farms; an ageing population; schools and shops closing
B1: the rural consequence explained, e.g. with fewer working-age people, local services lose customers and taxes and shut down
B1: an urban consequence identified, e.g. housing shortages; overcrowding; pressure on transport and services
B1: the urban consequence explained, e.g. demand for homes rises faster than building, so rents rise and informal settlements grow

long.q: A government plans to build a large dam on a river to generate electricity. Explain how the perspective of a farmer living in the valley that will be flooded might differ from the perspective of a factory owner in a city that needs more electricity. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the farmer is likely to oppose the dam
B1: reason explained, e.g. they would lose their land, home and income, and compensation may not replace them
B1: the factory owner is likely to support the dam
B1: reason explained, e.g. a reliable, cheaper electricity supply would cut power cuts and costs, so the business could grow

long.q: In Country X, the share of electricity generated from solar power rose from 2% in 2010 to 18% in 2023, while the share from coal fell from 70% to 45%. (a) Describe the trends shown by the data. (b) Suggest two possible reasons for these trends. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (a) solar increased by 16 percentage points (nine times its 2010 share)
B1: (a) coal fell by 25 percentage points but was still the larger source in 2023
B1: (b) a reason, e.g. solar panels have become much cheaper
B1: (b) a different reason, e.g. government targets or subsidies to cut carbon emissions; concern about air pollution from coal

long.q: Litter is a growing problem in many local parks. Propose one course of action to reduce it. Explain how your action would work and one possible consequence of carrying it out. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear, realistic course of action, e.g. more bins with separate recycling, plus fines for dropping litter
B1: who would carry it out and how, e.g. the council installs bins and wardens patrol at weekends
B1: why it would reduce litter, e.g. people drop less when a bin is close and when there is a real chance of a fine
B1: a consequence explained, e.g. cost to the council of emptying bins; or an unintended one, e.g. litter moves to streets outside the park

questions.q: A vested interest means
o: the author gains from persuading you
questions.why: e.g. a company reporting on its own product.

questions.q: How do you judge a source's reliability?
o: Check the author's expertise, purpose, evidence and date
questions.why: Bias and vested interest weaken reliability.

questions.q: What is a vested interest?
o: A personal stake that may bias a source
questions.why: For example a company writing about its own product.

questions.q: A study funded by a soft-drink company concludes that sugary drinks do not cause weight gain. What is the main reason to treat this source with caution?
o: It is about a health issue
The funder has a vested interest that may bias the findings
questions.why: The company gains if people believe its drinks are harmless, so the research may have been designed or reported to favour it.

questions.q: An article argues: 'Recycling is pointless, because my neighbour never bothers to recycle.' What is the main weakness of this argument?
o: It relies on too much statistical evidence
It generalises from a single personal example
It is written by an expert
questions.why: One neighbour's behaviour is not evidence about whether recycling as a whole is effective.

long.q: A source claims 'Electric cars will solve air pollution in cities'. Evaluate how convincing this claim is.
scheme: B1: identifies the claim and any evidence offered
B1: questions the source: author, purpose, vested interest
B1: weakness: pollution also from roads, tyres, industry, and electricity generation
B1: a reasoned judgement on how convincing it is

long.q: A blog post on the website of a company that sells water filters says: 'Tap water in our city is unsafe. Nine out of ten people we asked buy bottled water.' Explain two reasons why this source may not be reliable. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the company has a vested interest
B1: explained: it profits if people believe tap water is unsafe, so it may exaggerate
B1: the evidence is weak or unclear
B1: explained, e.g. we are not told how many people were asked or who they were; buying bottled water does not prove tap water is unsafe

long.q: Argument A: 'Schools should move to a four-day week. A trial in one district found pupils' attendance rose by 5%, and teachers said they felt less tired.' Argument B: 'A four-day week is a bad idea, because working parents would have to pay for childcare on the fifth day.' Which argument is more convincing? Explain your answer with reference to the evidence and reasoning in both. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a strength of A: it uses evidence from a trial (a measurable attendance figure)
B1: a weakness of A: one district may not be typical; teachers' feelings are opinion; nothing about learning or results
B1: a strength of B: it identifies a real, likely consequence for families
B1: a weakness of B: no evidence of how many families or what it would cost; it ignores any benefits
B1: a clear judgement on which is more convincing
B1: the judgement is justified by comparing the two, not just repeating one side

long.q: Explain what is meant by a 'vested interest', and explain how it can affect the credibility of a source. Use an example in your answer. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a vested interest is when the author or publisher gains (money, power, reputation) from people accepting a claim
B1: it reduces credibility because the source may select or exaggerate evidence that supports its own interest
B1: a suitable example, e.g. a sugar company funding research that says sugar is not linked to obesity

long.q: Someone argues: 'My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking can't be that harmful.' (a) Identify the weakness in this reasoning. (b) Suggest what kind of evidence would be more reliable for judging whether smoking is harmful. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (a) it generalises from a single case (anecdotal evidence)
B1: (a) explained: one person is not representative; many other smokers die younger
B1: (b) large-scale studies comparing the health of many smokers and non-smokers over many years, e.g. medical research published by health organisations

questions.q: Reflection in GP means
o: considering how your views and skills changed
questions.why: Reflect on what you learned and how.

questions.q: What should a personal reflection show?
o: How your thinking changed and what you learned
Only your opinion at the start
questions.why: Be specific about evidence that changed your mind.

questions.q: Which is reflective writing?
o: 'I first thought…, but the evidence on… made me reconsider because…'
questions.why: Reflection explains, not just describes.

questions.q: After a project on fast fashion, which statement best shows reflection on how the student's own perspective changed?
o: Fast fashion produces a large share of global carbon emissions.
Our group finished the project on time.
I used to buy cheap clothes without thinking, but learning about factory conditions has made me plan to buy fewer, longer-lasting items.
Everyone should stop buying new clothes.
questions.why: Reflection explains how and why the student's own views or behaviour changed as a result of the research.

questions.q: Which is the most useful reflection on the student's own teamwork skills?
o: I found it hard to speak up in meetings at first, so next time I will prepare my points in advance.
Our project was the best in the class.
questions.why: It identifies a specific weakness and sets out a realistic way to improve, which is what good reflection does.

questions.q: Good teamwork in the project means
o: agreeing roles and contributing to a shared outcome
questions.why: Collaboration is assessed.

questions.q: Why set roles in a team project?
o: So tasks are shared fairly and work is coordinated
questions.why: Evaluate how well the team worked.

questions.q: What is a good way to resolve disagreement in a team?
o: Discuss the evidence and agree a way forward
questions.why: Explain this in your reflection.

questions.q: In a team project, one member keeps missing deadlines. What is the most constructive first response?
o: Do their part without telling them
Report them to the teacher straight away
Talk with them to find out why and agree a realistic task and deadline
Remove their name from the project
questions.why: Discussing the problem openly keeps the member involved and solves the cause, which is the basis of good collaboration.

questions.q: Why might a team plan its project with a shared timeline showing a deadline for each task?
o: So that one person can control everything
So everyone knows what is due when and progress can be checked
So that the team does not need to discuss anything
So that the project takes longer
questions.why: A shared plan makes responsibilities and deadlines clear and lets the team spot problems early.

questions.q: A good written argument is
o: clear, structured and supported by evidence
questions.why: Structure and evidence persuade.

questions.q: What makes communication of an argument clear?
o: A logical structure with evidence for each point
questions.why: Know your audience.

questions.q: Why reference sources?
o: To show where evidence came from and let others check it
questions.why: Include author, title, date and link.

questions.q: Which sentence best supports a claim with evidence?
o: Phones are obviously bad for learning.
Phones are distracting and annoying in class.
Phones distract students: in our survey of 120 students, 70% said they check messages during lessons.
questions.why: It backs the claim with specific data and says where the data came from.

questions.q: A student is giving a presentation on saving water to a class of 8-year-olds. Which approach is most effective?
o: Reading a long report word for word
Using as much technical vocabulary as possible
Simple language, a clear structure and a few striking visuals
Including every fact the student found
questions.why: Effective communication is adapted to its audience; young children need clear, simple and visual information.

long.q: Write a short structured argument (about 150 words) on whether schools should ban mobile phones during lessons. Support your reasons with evidence, respond to another perspective, and reach a conclusion. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear position stated at the start
B1: reasons supported by evidence or specific examples
B1: an opposing perspective acknowledged and answered
B1: a conclusion that follows from the reasoning, in clear, organised paragraphs

long.q: Rewrite this paragraph so that it is clearer, more objective and better organised for a report: 'Plastic is literally destroying everything. Loads of it ends up in the sea and fish eat it and it's awful. Everyone knows we need to stop using it right now, and people who don't care are ridiculous.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: emotive and exaggerated language removed (e.g. 'literally destroying everything', 'ridiculous')
B1: informal words replaced with formal ones (e.g. 'loads of' → 'large amounts of')
B1: the claim is linked to evidence or a source, or presented as a claim to be supported
B1: logically ordered sentences: problem, effect, suggested action, with linking words

long.q: Write a short proposal (about 120 words) to your head teacher for a school vegetable garden. Include its aim, how it would be set up and run, one benefit, and one challenge with a way to overcome it. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear aim stated at the start
B1: a practical plan for setting it up and running it (where, who, when)
B1: a benefit explained, e.g. pupils learn where food comes from; produce used in the canteen
B1: a challenge with a realistic solution, e.g. watering in holidays → a rota of families
B1: a formal, polite tone suited to the head teacher, organised in short paragraphs

long.q: Read this passage and summarise its main points in no more than 40 words: 'Fast fashion has made clothes cheaper than ever. Many shoppers now buy new outfits every month and throw them away after a few wears. Making clothes uses huge amounts of water and energy, and much discarded clothing ends up in landfill. Some brands now offer repair services and take back old clothes for recycling, and some shoppers are choosing second-hand clothes instead.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: cheap clothes mean people buy often and discard quickly
B1: environmental impact: water and energy use, and landfill
B1: responses: repair and take-back schemes, or second-hand buying
B1: in your own words, no more than 40 words, no new opinions added

long.q: Explain two features that help a reader follow a written argument, and say why each one helps. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a feature, e.g. a clear statement of the writer's position in the introduction
B1: why it helps, e.g. the reader knows from the start what the evidence is meant to support
B1: a second feature, e.g. one main point per paragraph with linking words (however, therefore)
B1: why it helps, e.g. the reader can see how each point builds towards the conclusion
